kaggle_handle.reasoning: The Kaggle mirror 'Daily cash and debt operations of U.S. Treasury' of the Daily Treasury Statement (US government data, 2005-10-03 to 2023-04-03): the Treasury's deposits and withdrawals of operating cash per business day, a real daily cashflow record with the inflow / outflow / balance structure of a corporate cash account, chosen as the rehearsal for daily cashflow forecasting.

raw_file.reasoning: The reduced table make data keeps: per business day, account and transaction type, the day's amount in millions USD, summed over the statement's categories (sub-total rows dropped). The full deposits-and-withdrawals table is 55 MB, too large to commit; the reduced one is under 300 KB and holds everything the builder needs.

value_columns.reasoning: The running totals of deposits and of withdrawals since the first day, in billions USD. Cumulating makes the series I(1) by construction and positive, so the pipeline's first differences are the daily flows, every model and transform applies unchanged, and the error of a level forecast h days ahead is the error of the h-day total. Their difference is the change in the cash balance, which links the two series as the balance sheet's two series were linked.

unit_suffix.reasoning: The columns are tagged with their unit, billions; chart titles drop the tag.

unit.reasoning: Billions of USD: the statement reports millions, and daily flows of 20 to 500 billion read more easily in billions.

title.value: U.S. Treasury operating cash: cumulative deposits and withdrawals
title.reasoning: The series plot's title: what the two series describe.

train_percent.reasoning: The project's rule for every model: 60 / 20 / 20 train / validation / test, in time order, never shuffled. Whole percentages, so the split boundaries use exact integer arithmetic.

validation_percent.reasoning: Same rule: validation selects models; test takes the remaining 20% and is run once per model family.

alias.reasoning: pandas' business-day alias: the statement is published on business days, and the builder puts a zero flow on the weekdays without a statement (holidays). Every fifth row is then the same weekday, which the seasonal period of 5, the seasonal naive and the weekday profile rely on; skipping holidays would shift the weekday rhythm by one position at each.

period.reasoning: The word for one step of the series in reports and figure titles ('5 days ahead', 'an origin every 20 days'): the rows are business days.

date_format.reasoning: How reports print a date: daily observations need the day.

significance_level.reasoning: The conventional 5% level, used by every test and confidence band so verdicts are comparable across steps. Johansen's critical-value tables exist only at 10%, 5% and 1%.

max_acf_lags.reasoning: Twelve weeks of daily lags, so the weekly rhythm (lags 5, 10, 15, ...) and the month-end rhythm (about lags 21 and 42) both show in the ACF / PACF.

max_order_sum.reasoning: The project's grid rule (2026-10-23): every (p, q) with p + d + q <= 5, a total-complexity budget that covers pure AR, pure MA and mixed models alike.

differencing_order.reasoning: ADF and KPSS agree on train: both series are I(1), and one difference makes them stationary. Applied by fitting on the first differences.

seasonal_ar_orders.reasoning: No seasonal term or one, as for the monthly data: a second weekly coefficient at lag 10 is covered by the non-seasonal orders up to 4 together with one seasonal term. No seasonal differencing, since one regular difference already gives stationarity (the flows).

seasonal_ma_orders.reasoning: As for the seasonal AR orders: none or one seasonal MA term.

seasonal_period.reasoning: Business-day data: the seasonal cycle is one week of five business days (holidays are zero-flow days, so the cycle keeps its length).

max_iterations.reasoning: Four times statsmodels' default of 50, so slow but sound likelihood fits finish. Fits that still don't converge are counted and reported, never hidden.

adf_autolag.reasoning: statsmodels' default: the ADF lag length chosen by AIC (Said and Dickey 1984), so leftover serial correlation doesn't distort the test.

kpss_nlags.reasoning: The data-dependent bandwidth of Hobijn, Franses and Ooms (1998), statsmodels' recommended setting for the KPSS long-run variance.

pacf_method.reasoning: Yule-Walker with MLE scaling: its PACF never exceeds 1 in size, and it is what statsmodels' PACF plots use, so the report's table matches the figure.

test_lags.reasoning: One, two and four weeks: short-run, weekly and month-long autocorrelation left in the SARIMA residuals.

aic_tie_margin.reasoning: Burnham and Anderson (2002): a model within 2 AIC of the best still has substantial support, so the runner-up is checked too.

plot_lags.reasoning: Display only: four weeks of lags in the ACF and Ljung-Box panels, up to the longest test lag.

arch_test_lags.reasoning: Yesterday, one week and two weeks: short-lived and persistent volatility clustering.

plot_lags.reasoning: Display only: every ARCH-LM lag up to the longest test lag, two weeks.

max_lags.reasoning: VAR lag orders 0..10 tried, two weeks of daily lags: at 10 lags each equation has 20 lag coefficients plus a constant, from about 2,730 usable training days, about 125 observations per coefficient.

primary_criterion.reasoning: BIC drives the Johansen decision: it is consistent (picks the true order as the sample grows), which suits a question about the model's structure.

test_lags.reasoning: One, two and four weeks, as in the univariate residual checks.

plot_lags.reasoning: Display only: four weeks of lags, up to the longest test lag.

horizon.reasoning: Four weeks after the shock: long enough for daily responses to settle and to show one month-end.

report_horizons.reasoning: The impact day, one week, two weeks and the end of the response window.

band_z.reasoning: The standard normal's 97.5% quantile, rounded as usual: value +- 1.96 standard errors is a 95% band, matching the 5% significance level.

half_width.reasoning: A 21-day window, four weeks and a day: each weekday appears four times, so the weekday profile's median rests on four values, and the window is shorter than the month-to-month drift of the flows.

seasonal_profile.reasoning: Daily flows have a strong weekday rhythm (Thursday settlements of Treasury securities are several times the other days' flows), so a plain rolling median would flag every Thursday and clipping would erase the rhythm the models must learn. threshold.reasoning: The Hampel filter's usual cut-off (Pearson 2002): with the median absolute deviation scaled by 1.4826 to estimate the standard deviation of normal data, 3 flags about 0.3% of ordinary changes.

huber_delta.reasoning: Huber's constant for 95% efficiency under normal errors (Huber 1981): squared loss for errors within 1.345 standard deviations of the standardized target, absolute beyond, so extreme days pull the fit linearly instead of quadratically.

horizons.reasoning: One day, one week, two weeks and 21 business days (30 calendar days), the shortest planning horizon the cashflow application needs. quantiles.reasoning: The median and the ends of the 80% and 95% central intervals, the two interval levels most used in forecast evaluation. validation_step.reasoning: An origin every 40 business days (about two months) through the 913 validation days gives 23 expanding-window folds, above the 10 the validation rule asks for and more than the monthly benchmark's 14; each fits on every day from the start of the data to its origin and forecasts the validation days up to 21 ahead, so every horizon is scored at every fold. candidates.reasoning: Optuna trials per model.
